name: ConsensusRecSplit
workload: Single-threaded construction of MPHFs over 100 million random string keys (uniform random length 10-50), plotting space overhead (bits/key) against construction throughput for ConsensusRecSplit versus RecSplit, SIMDRecSplit, ShockHash-RS and bipartite ShockHash-RS/-Flat.
claimed_speedup: Against RecSplit (paper Table 1, 100M random string keys, single-threaded): RecSplit l=12,b=2000 reaches 1.613 bits/key at 25,667 ns/key construction. ConsensusRecSplit k=256,eps=0.1 reaches 1.578 bits/key at 248 ns/key, about 103x faster construction at lower space (derived from page data). ConsensusRecSplit k=32768,eps=0.0005 reaches 1.444 bits/key at 30,245 ns/key, roughly the same time RecSplit needs for 1.613 bits/key. The paper's '>350x faster at 1.489 bits/key' is against bipartite ShockHash-RS (the previous most space-efficient approach), not RecSplit. The project README separately states that on 100M keys, with about an hour of construction, it reaches 1.4448 bits/key (lower bound 1.4427) where RecSplit reaches 1.6127 bits/key.
compiler_and_flags: GNU C++ 11.2.0, -O3 -march=native
hardware: Intel i7-11700, 2.5GHz base clock, 48KiB/512KiB L1/L2 per core, 16MiB L3
tradeoffs: Very slow in absolute terms at maximum space-efficiency settings (~1 hour for 100M keys); needs a large bucket size (e.g. k=32768) for the best trade-off; combines with a separate threshold-based k-perfect hash layer for cache locality, adding implementation complexity; GPL-3.0 + runtime exception licensing.
caveats: The comparison is by the ConsensusRecSplit authors (their MPHF-Experiments framework), single-threaded, on 100M string keys. The headline '>350x' figure is against bipartite ShockHash-RS, not RecSplit. Queries are not faster: 140-217 ns vs RecSplit's 139-156 ns in Table 1. The paper includes only approaches below 1.6 bits/key, so it has no BBHash/CMPH/PTHash comparison. The latest GitHub release (tag 2026-01-04) points at the 2025-06-23 commit.

name: emphf

claimed_speedup: On mphf_benchmark (PTHash SIGIR'21 Table 5, 1 billion random 64-bit keys, single core, i9-9900K), emphf builds in 374 s at 2.61 bits/key. CMPH's CHD needs 1972 / 5964 / 23746 s for lambda=4/5/6 (2.17/2.07/2.01 bits/key), so emphf builds about 5.3-63x faster (derived from page data). emphf lookups take 199 ns/key vs CHD's 416-419 ns/key, about 2.1x faster (derived from page data), but emphf uses 0.4-0.6 more bits/key. Separately, the rchikhi/benchmphf README reports emphf's HEM variant building a 1-billion-key MPHF in 770 s using 24 GB, vs the 'phf' library's 3900 s and 48 GB, about 5x faster (derived from page data); that page gives no CMPH numbers.

hardware: Intel i9-9900K @3.60GHz, 64GB DDR3 RAM @2.66GHz, Linux 5 (64-bit)
tradeoffs: Noticeably slower lookup (199 ns/key) than BBHash or PTHash in the same table; external-memory scan_mmap mode trades speed for lower construction memory; predates BBHash (2017) and PTHash (2021), so it was never tuned against them.
caveats: The benchmark is the PTHash authors' harness, not emphf's own. emphf builds and looks up faster than CMPH's CHD but uses more space (2.61 vs 2.01-2.17 bits/key). name: LeMonHash
baseline: Prior monotone MPHF implementations: the Grossi-Ottaviano C++ Centroid Hollow Trie, Hollow Trie and Path Decomposed Trie (ot/path_decomposed_tries), plus the Belazzougui et al. Java implementations from Sux4J of the Hollow Trie Distributor, Hollow Trie, ZFast Trie, LCP, LCP 2-step, PaCo, VLLCP and VLPaCo
workload: Rank queries (monotone minimal perfect hashing) over synthetic 64-bit integer datasets (uniform/normal/exponential, 100M keys) and real-world datasets (text, dna, urls, 5gram, fb, osm; 35M-800M keys), measuring query throughput, construction throughput, and bits/key vs prior MMPHF techniques
claimed_speedup: Abstract: on synthetic random integers, 34% less space than the next larger competitor with about 16x faster queries; on real-world data, up to 19x faster queries than the next larger competitor at similar or better space; up to 2x faster construction than the competitor with the next best space usage (typically Hollow Trie variants); LeMonHash-VL (strings) is within 13% of the best competitors' space with up to 3x faster queries than the next larger competitor. Derived from page data (Table A.1): on uniform keys, 2718 vs 179 kQueries/s = 15.2x against the Java (Sux4J) Hollow Trie at 2.98 vs 4.54 bits/key; against the C++ Hollow Trie (351 kq/s, 4.61 bpk) it is 7.7x; on osm, 1338 vs 73 kq/s = 18.3x against the Java HTDist.
compiler_and_flags: GNU C++ 11.1.0, -O3 -march=native
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2670 v3 @ 2.3GHz, Ubuntu 20.04, Linux 5.10.0, single-threaded
tradeoffs: GPLv3 is copyleft (no permissive reuse in proprietary code); like all MPHFs it returns arbitrary output for keys outside the original set; monotone MPHFs preserve key order (unlike plain MPHFs), which is a narrower guarantee that costs more space than a non-order-preserving MPHF; needs epsilon tuning for the PGM bucket mapper and depends on the BuRR retrieval structure and PGM-index as building blocks
caveats: The headline 16x and 19x ratios are against Java (Sux4J) implementations, run on OpenJDK 17 with one unmeasured JIT warm-up run. Against the fastest C++ competitor at similar space, the gap is about 7-8x (derived from Table A.1). The comparison covers only academic MMPHF implementations, not BBHash, CMPH, PTHash, std::map or a sorted-array binary search. An MMPHF preserves key order (it returns the key's rank), so it is a different problem from a plain MPHF. The integer variant supports integer keys only; LeMonHash-VL covers strings. The Path Decomposed Trie crashes on integer inputs. Each experiment ran only twice and was averaged (the paper says variation is small).

name: PHast / PHast+ (bsuccinct-rs "ph" crate)
workload: MPHF-Experiments framework: MPHF construction (1 and 12 threads) and queries on 5*10^7 and 5*10^8 random string keys, each of uniformly random length 10-50 bytes (Tables 5.2/5.3 of arXiv:2504.17918). Uniformly random 64-bit integer keys were used only for parameter tuning (Sec. 5.1) and the ablation study (Sec. 5.4). Measures bits/key, query ns/query, and construction ns/key.
claimed_speedup: At 5*10^7 keys: PHast (S=8, lambda=4.3, EF) reaches 1.94 bit/key, 10 ns/key query, 606 ns/key single-thread construction (69 ns/key at 12 threads), vs PTHash (lambda=5.0, EF) at 2.11 bit/key, 54 ns/key query, 577 ns/key construction (231 ns/key at 12 threads); PHast+ cuts single-thread construction to 61-140 ns/key (an order of magnitude faster than PHast) for 10-15 ns/key query (derived from page data, Table 5.2 of arXiv:2504.17918)
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.84.1 and gcc 12.2.0, both with third-level (-O3-equivalent) and CPU-native optimizations enabled
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5600G @ 3.9 GHz, 6 cores / 12 threads, 384KB/3MB/16MB L1/L2/L3 cache
tradeoffs: PHast/PHast+ trade small space overhead (~1.8-2.3 bits/key) for very simple, fast bucket-placement queries; PHast+ construction is 5-9x faster than PHast single-threaded and parallelizes near-linearly; PtrHash overtakes PHast on very large key sets once evaluation becomes memory-bandwidth bound. The same crate also ships FMPH/FMPHGO, fingerprinting-based MPHFs designed as a faster/smaller alternative to BBHash.
caveats: First-party paper by the PHast authors (Beling, Sanders); the ph crate author is the first author. At 5*10^7 keys, single-thread PHast construction (606 ns/key for S=8, lambda=4.3, EF) is slightly slower than PTHash (577 ns/key). PHast wins on query time (10 vs 54 ns), space (1.94 vs 2.11 bits/key), and 12-thread construction (69 vs 231 ns/key). PtrHash is close on queries, and at 5*10^8 keys it catches up with and may overtake PHast+ (3.2). The comparison is only against other MPHFs (PTHash, PTHash-HEM, PHOBIC, PtrHash, SIMDRecSplit, SicHash, FMPH, FMPHGO, FiPS, Bipartite ShockHash). It does not compare against std::unordered_map or CMPH. The paper left BBHash out of its tests because FMPH is its improved counterpart. GitHub's license detector reports only Apache-2.0, but the README and ph/Cargo.toml state the dual license 'MIT OR Apache-2.0'.

name: PTHash
workload: Construction and lookup of MPHFs over 1 billion uniformly random 64-bit integer keys, single core (construction and lookup single-threaded; BBHash also run with one thread), reproducing Table 5 of the PTHash SIGIR'21 paper.
claimed_speedup: At similar space (~3 bits/key) on 1 billion random 64-bit keys, single core, PTHash lookups take 37 ns/key (C-C, alpha=0.99, c=7, 3.23 bits/key) and 55 ns/key (D-D, alpha=0.94, c=7, 2.99 bits/key), vs 170 ns/key for BBHash gamma=1 (3.06 bits/key). That is about 3.1-4.6x faster lookups (derived from page data); the paper text says 3-4.5x vs BBHash gamma=1,2. BBHash builds faster at that setting (253 s vs 689-1042 s for these PTHash variants).

hardware: Intel i9-9900K @3.60GHz, 64GB DDR3 RAM @2.66GHz, Linux 5 (64-bit)
tradeoffs: Offline/batch construction only (not incremental); needs a 64-bit-bucket-id compile flag beyond 2^32 buckets; several encoder/bucketer configs (lambda, alpha, dense vs partitioned) must be tuned for the desired space/time trade-off.

name: RSHash
workload: Streaming and single k-mer lookup/build over large k-mer sets (genome datasets from Pibiri 2022), comparing a rank/select-bitvector hash construction against SSHash's PTHash-based dictionary.
claimed_speedup: Streaming lookups: RSHash is on average 1.4x and up to 2x faster than SSHash5. It queries 4.5x more k-mers/s on average, and up to 8.5x more, than the published SSHash3 (Table 4, Fig. 4). Single-k-mer lookups are on par with SSHash5: 0.5 us/k-mer (fast variant) and 0.6 us/k-mer (compact variant). Negative lookups are 50% faster and positive lookups are 10% slower (Table 5). Build is on average 60% faster with 40% less memory (Table 6; human 3:23 and 10.4 GB vs SSHash5 6:03 and 14.4 GB). All figures are verbatim from the paper.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 12.2, release mode (paper); source/CMakeLists.txt sets -O3 -march=native
hardware: AMD EPYC 9454 @ 2.75 GHz, 1 TB RAM, single core, Debian (kernel 6.1.0-43), 64-bit
tradeoffs: Uses succinct rank/select bitvectors rather than a classical MPHF construction, so it is a competing technique in the same k-mer-dictionary space rather than an MPHF library itself; specialized to DNA k-mers, not general-purpose keys; very new/low-adoption project.
caveats: The baseline is SSHash, another k-mer dictionary, not std::unordered_map, CMPH, BBHash or any MPHF. RSHash itself replaces the MPHF with rank/select bitvectors. Positive random single-k-mer lookups are 10% slower than SSHash5. test/hashtable.cpp can time std::unordered_set<uint64_t> streaming lookups, but no such numbers are published, and the benchmarks README describes that file as a correctness check. The repo was created 2025-02-17, not Feb 2026. It has 8 stars.
found_via: Blogs / talks: found while following the k-mer MPHF blog trail from Camille Marchet's page and the SSHash lineage of papers; confirmed via the peer-reviewed RSHash paper (Bioinformatics 2026) and its GitHub repo/README.

name: ShockHash
workload: Single-threaded construction of MPHFs for 10 million keys, which are random strings of uniform length 10-50 (not 64-bit integers). ShockHash-RS, RecSplit, SIMDRecSplit and others are compared at matched space (~1.56-1.59 bits/key) on construction ns/key and query ns/key (paper Table 1).
claimed_speedup: At 1.56 bits/key, ShockHash-RS (n=39, b=2000) builds at 1,805 ns/key (1.556 bits/key), which the paper calls 'about 75 times faster than the next competitor' (SIMDRecSplit n=16, b=2000: 1.560 bits/key at 137,902 ns/key). Against plain RecSplit (n=14, b=2000: 1.585 bits/key, 125,521 ns/key), ShockHash-RS n=30, b=2000 builds at 787 ns/key for 1.583 bits/key, about 160x faster at equal space (derived from page data). Queries are slightly slower (114-118 ns vs 97 ns).
compiler_and_flags: GNU C++ 11.2.0, -O3 -march=native
hardware: Intel i7-11700, 8 cores, 2.5GHz base, Ubuntu 22.04
tradeoffs: Base case is exponential-time in theory (mitigated by integrating into RecSplit-style partitioning); space-optimal configurations still take much longer to build than fingerprinting methods in absolute terms; SIMD variants need AVX support; GPL-3.0 + runtime exception licensing.
caveats: The main numeric win is against RecSplit/SIMDRecSplit, not the category incumbents. CHD (CMPH) appears only as a curve in the Figure 5 Pareto plot, with no tabulated numbers. BBHash is omitted because FMPH (Rust) 'significantly outperforms' it. All runs are single-threaded. The MPHF-Experiments harness has since been updated for the bipartite-ShockHash paper (src/tableShockHash.cpp), so reproducing Table 1 exactly needs the 2023 commit.

name: SimdRecSplit / GpuRecSplit
workload: Single-threaded MPHF construction for 10 million keys, which are random strings of uniform length 10-50 (not 64-bit integers). SIMDRecSplit is compared against BBHash, RecSplit, PTHash and SicHash on bits/key and construction/query ns per key (paper Table 3). The GPU and multi-core speedups come from paper Table 1 (5 million objects, random 128-bit master hash codes, relative to the original single-threaded RecSplit).
claimed_speedup: Single-threaded on 10M keys, SIMDRecSplit (l=5, b=5) builds in 49 ns/key at 2.96 bits/key. BBHash gamma=1.0 needs 208 ns/key at 3.059 bits/key, so SIMDRecSplit is about 4.2x faster and smaller (derived from page data). BBHash gamma=5.0 is about as fast (50 ns/key) but needs 6.871 bits/key. Against the original RecSplit, speedups reach 50x single-threaded SIMD, 239x with 16 threads and 5438x on an RTX 3090 GPU (l=18, b=50, 5M objects; paper Table 1).
compiler_and_flags: GNU C++ (gcc) 11.2.0, -O3 -march=native; CUDA 11 for the GPU variant
hardware: Intel i7-11700 (8 cores/16 threads, 2.5GHz base, AVX-512); NVIDIA RTX 3090 for the GPU variant
tradeoffs: GPU variant requires CUDA hardware/drivers; SIMD variant needs AVX support (falls back to slower emulated SIMD without it); licensed GPL-3.0 + GCC Runtime Library Exception (same terms as libstdc++), which is more restrictive than BBHash's/PTHash's permissive licenses.
caveats: The BBHash numbers were checked by hand against the Table 3 PDF (v2, 5 Jul 2023) and match. Table 3 runs BBHash single-threaded. BBHash is a parallel code, but Figure 6 shows it scales poorly, so this does not flip the result. SIMDRecSplit queries are slower than BBHash (71 vs 51 ns/key at the compared settings). The README's headline table compares only against RecSplit. The SIMD path targets x86 AVX-512/AVX2, and the GPU path needs CUDA.

claimed_speedup: Human dataset, canonical SSHash, from Tables 4-7. Streaming membership: 253 ns/k-mer (high-hit) vs Pufferfish dense 402 and Blight b=0 440; 183 ns/k-mer (low-hit) vs 435 and 1,088. The paper summarizes this as 'comparable to or faster (by 2-3x) than Pufferfish and Blight'. Space: 9.39 bits/k-mer vs Pufferfish dense 45.04 and Blight b=0 20.17. Build: 16.2 min and 17.3 GB peak vs Pufferfish dense 70.7 min and 14.0 GB, and Blight 25.0 min and 7.5 GB. Random lookups: 990 ns positive and 854 ns negative, which is slower than Pufferfish dense (720 and 519) but faster than Blight b=0 (1,780 and 1,610).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 11.2.0, -O3 -march=native
hardware: Intel Core i9-9940X @ 3.30 GHz, 128 GB RAM, single core used; Ubuntu 19.10, Linux kernel 5.3.0, 64-bit
tradeoffs: Specialized to fixed-length DNA k-mer keys (not a general-purpose MPHF library); static/immutable once built; relies on PTHash internally so inherits its construction-time/space tradeoffs; needs minimizer sampling tuned per dataset.
caveats: All comparisons are against other k-mer dictionaries (dBG-FM, Pufferfish, BLight; later SBWT and FMSI), never against std::unordered_map, CMPH, BBHash or a bare MPHF. name: BLight
workload: Exact associative index over k-mers of the human genome (k=31): build the index and answer membership/identifier queries over the full reference, using an MPHF (BBHash-style) plus minimizer indexing.
claimed_speedup: Human genome, k=31. Table 1 (construction): BLight 10 min, 7.4 GB peak, 22.3 bits/k-mer vs Pufferfish dense 69 min, 27.4 GB, 55.59 bits/k-mer. BLight ran with 12 threads; its single-thread human build took 60 min. Table 2 (querying all reference k-mers): BLight 1,748 s single-thread vs Pufferfish '1.799' (presumably 1,799 s), and 155 s multi-threaded vs 655 s. The column is labelled 16T, but the text says 12 threads. On real reads (SRR5833294), single-thread BLight takes 1,577 s vs Pufferfish 1,260 s, so BLight is slower there. All figures are verbatim from the paper.

hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2420 @ 1.90 GHz, 192 GB RAM, Ubuntu 16.04
tradeoffs: AGPL-3.0 is copyleft and network-use-triggering, a stronger restriction than most catalog entries; specialized to k-mer/genomics keys; static index (no updates) as opposed to Bifrost's dynamic index.
caveats: BLight is compared only against Pufferfish, a k-mer index, not against std::unordered_map, BBHash or CMPH directly. The construction win compares BLight on 12 threads against Pufferfish. Single-thread queries are at parity on reference k-mers, and BLight is slower than Pufferfish on real reads (1,577 vs 1,260 s). name: Engineering Minimal/k-Perfect Hash Functions (stefanfred implementation)
baseline: CMPH CHD (cmph library, run as non-minimal k-perfect with load factor 0.97, because cmph CHD supports only non-minimal k-perfect hashing) and the ad-hoc threshold-based bumping kPHF from CONSENSUS-RecSplit [30]; no BBHash, PTHash or 1-perfect RecSplit comparison
workload: Minimal k-perfect hash function construction and queries for k = 10, 100 and 1000 on 100 million random strings of uniform random length in [10, 50]. Figure 5 plots space vs construction and query throughput; Table 2 lists representative configurations for k = 10 and k = 1000. There are no k = 1 (standard MPHF) experiments.
claimed_speedup: Abstract: 'Our implementations simultaneously dominate older approaches in space consumption, construction time, and query time.' Table 2, k = 10: CHD (load factor 0.97) 0.627 bits/key, 495 ns/key construction, 96 ns/query; Threshold-Based 0.716 bits/key, 77 ns/key, 56 ns/query; Bucket Placement (Compact) 1.917 bits/key, 584 ns/key, 47 ns/query; Threshold-Based + Consensus 0.450 bits/key, 233 ns/key, 57 ns/query (better than CHD on all three). That is about 6.4x faster construction (Threshold-Based vs CHD) and 1.7x-2.0x faster queries (derived from page data). Text: up to 3 times smaller space overhead than the ad-hoc threshold-based implementation, and up to 50% faster construction than the next best technique. The CHD implementation crashes for k = 1000. Query times are 22-291 ns/query, not single-digit nanoseconds.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.2.0, -O3 -march=native
hardware: Intel i7 11700 (8 cores, 2.5 GHz base clock), Rocky Linux 9.5, Linux 5.14.0
tradeoffs: Very new, low-adoption research code (1 star); generalizes to k-perfect hashing (buckets may hold up to k keys), of which minimal perfect hashing is the k=1 special case; GPL-3.0 is copyleft.
caveats: ESA 2025 paper (LIPIcs vol. 351, 99:1-99:18, DOI 10.4230/LIPIcs.ESA.2025.99; software artifact DOI 10.4230/artifacts.24698). This is a k-perfect hashing library (k = 10/100/1000 evaluated), not a 1-perfect MPHF. It is not compared against BBHash, PTHash or 1-perfect RecSplit. The only external baselines are cmph CHD, run non-minimal at load factor 0.97 and crashing at k = 1000, and the ad-hoc threshold-based bumping from CONSENSUS-RecSplit. CHD is slightly smaller than plain Threshold-Based at k = 10 (0.627 vs 0.716 bits/key), but Threshold-Based + Consensus beats CHD on space, construction and query. Table 2 is plain text in the PDF, not images. GPL-3.0 applies.

name: LPHash
workload: An MPHF over the distinct k-mers of 5 whole-genome datasets, from Yeast (11.6M k-mers) to Human (2.77G k-mers), given as spectrum-preserving string sets (BCALM2 + UST stitched unitigs), for k=31..63. Space is measured in bits/k-mer. Queries are about 100M k-mers from human chr13, measured in streaming and random order on a single core.
claimed_speedup: Paper Table 3: partitioned LPHash at k=63 uses 0.53, 0.64, 0.83, 0.58 and 0.87 bits/k-mer on Yeast, Elegans, Cod, Kestrel and Human. BBHash-v1 uses 3.71 bits/k-mer, BBHash-v2 3.06, PTHash-v1 2.58-2.76 and PTHash-v2 2.04-2.20. The paper states LPHash is 5.1x, 4.1x, 3.2x, 4.4x and 3x smaller than PTHash-v1 and 2.3-3.7x smaller than PTHash-v2. Against BBHash-v2 it is about 3.5-5.8x smaller (derived from page data). At k=31, LPHash uses 1.18-1.74 bits/k-mer. For streaming queries the paper says: 'Compared to BBHash, LPHash is 2x faster on Yeast and up to 4-5x faster on the larger datasets.' The README's claim of '< 0.9 bits/k-mer vs 1.44 lower bound and 2-3 bits/k-mer for practical constructions' matches these tables.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 11.2.0, -O3 -march=native (paper). The repo CMakeLists.txt also adds -std=c++17 -mbmi2 -msse4.2.
hardware: Intel i9-9900K @ 3.60 GHz, 64 GB RAM, Linux 5.13.0. Queries ran on 1 core. Builds used 4 threads.
tradeoffs: Specialized for consecutive/overlapping k-mer key sets in bioinformatics, not a general-purpose MPHF; requires k-mer-specific preprocessing (stitched unitig files); partitioned vs. unpartitioned construction is a further trade-off between memory and speed.
caveats: The space win applies only to overlapping k-mers from spectrum-preserving string sets. The paper stresses that BBHash and PTHash are general-purpose MPHFs for arbitrary keys. Random-order (non-streaming) queries are slower than PTHash. Construction is slower than BBHash-v1: Table 5 gives 05:30 vs 00:48 on Cod and 07:25 vs 04:13 on Human. Datasets are on Zenodo (record 7239205). The last commit on the default branch (main) is 2023-07-19. The dev branch has a later commit, dated 2023-11-18.

name: MorphisHash
workload: (1) A single Bipartite MorphisHash vs Bipartite ShockHash base case (n up to about 64 keys): idealized space overhead and average successful seed (Figs. 2-3). (2) Partitioned MorphisHash-RS/-Flat vs Bipartite ShockHash-RS/-Flat (and CONSENSUS-RS, PHOBIC) on 100 million keys in the MPHF-Experiments framework: space (bits/key), query time (ns/query) and construction time (ns/key) (Table 1, Fig. 5).
claimed_speedup: Abstract: MorphisHash saves Theta(ln n) bits in expectation vs ShockHash, 'a factor of 20 less space overhead in practice'. That factor is for a single unpartitioned base case (Sec. 6.1, Bipartite MorphisHash with b=n-6): under 0.1 bits of total overhead vs about 2 bits for Bipartite ShockHash, at the cost of about 4x more seed tests. For a full MPHF on 100M keys (Table 1), Bip. MorphisHash-RS (n=52, b=n-4) gives 1.501 bits/key, 137 ns/query and 6,669 ns/key construction. Bip. ShockHash-RS (n=66) gives 1.523 bits/key, 147 ns/query and 7,186 ns/key. This is about 0.02 bits/key, or 27% less overhead, at equal construction time. At an equal 1.489 bits/key, MorphisHash-RS builds in 8,085 ns/key vs 172,738 ns/key for ShockHash-RS, which the paper calls about 21x faster construction.
hardware: Intel Core i7-11700 (48 KiB L1d and 512 KiB L2 per core, 16 MiB L3), 64 GiB dual-channel DDR4-3200
tradeoffs: GitHub fork of ByteHamster/ShockHash that changes the seed-encoding scheme to remove redundant key-to-position mappings, reducing space at the same query complexity; integrated as its own contender in ByteHamster/MPHF-Experiments; very low external adoption (3 stars) despite the algorithmic improvement
caveats: The '20x less space overhead' figure applies to the per-base-case redundancy of ShockHash, not to total bits/key. For full 100M-key MPHFs, the gain is about 0.01-0.02 bits/key at equal construction time, or about 21x faster construction at equal space (1.489 bits/key). The paper does not state the compiler or flags; the MorphisHash and MPHF-Experiments CMake files default to a Release build with -march=native. The baseline (ShockHash) is an advanced research MPHF by the same group, not std::unordered_map, CMPH or BBHash. Single-author paper that uses the group's own benchmark framework. name: PHOBIC-GPU
workload: MPHF construction on 100 million random string keys (random length 10-50 characters). GPU construction (plus 8 CPU threads) is compared with CPU PHOBIC at 1 and 8 threads, for the same configurations (lambda=9, 13, 14; interleaved Rice/Compact coding). All queries run on the CPU.
claimed_speedup: PHOBIC-GPU constructs an MPHF at 2.17 bits/key in 28 ns/key (GPU + 8 CPU threads), and the MPHF answers queries in 37 ns on the CPU (abstract, Table 1). At lambda=9.0 with interleaved Rice coding, PHOBIC-GPU gives 1.76 bits/key, 52 ns/query and 27 ns/key construction. CPU PHOBIC gives 1.74 bits/key, 50 ns/query, 9,171 ns/key (1 thread) and 1,781 ns/key (8 threads). The paper states a 62x construction speedup over the multithreaded CPU implementation and about 30x lower energy (Table 1, Sec. 5.2 of arXiv:2404.18497).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.4.0, -march=native -O3; GPU accessed via Vulkan 1.3.236
hardware: Intel Core i7-11700 (48 KiB L1d and 512 KiB L2 per core), 64 GiB DDR4, Ubuntu 22.04.1; GPU: Nvidia RTX 3090
tradeoffs: Requires Vulkan-capable GPU for construction; only construction is GPU-accelerated, queries still run on CPU; the CPU PHOBIC implementation it accelerates lives inside the already-catalogued jermp/pthash repo (branch 'phobic'), so this repo only supplies the GPU construction path
caveats: The speedup compares an RTX 3090 GPU with an 8-thread i7-11700 CPU, so it depends on the hardware. The paper notes the GPU only wins for large n and large lambda; at small lambda, transferring the input to the GPU dominates. Queries are not faster: they run on the CPU and are the same as CPU PHOBIC. The system draws about 405 W during the GPU search vs 195 W for the multithreaded CPU. Needs a Vulkan-capable GPU. name: PtrHash
baseline: BBHash and CMPH (CHD) in the arXiv 2506.06536 survey; PTHash and PHOBIC (plus CMPH CHD) in the SEA 2025 paper arXiv 2502.15539
workload: Survey Table 6: 100M random strings of length 10-50, single-threaded construction, then 100M queries, via MPHF-Experiments tableSurvey. SEA 2025 paper Table 2: 300M random strings of length 10-50 via MPHF-Experiments, 6-thread construction where supported. SEA 2025 paper Table 1: 1e9 random 64-bit integer keys hashed with FxHash, for-loop and prefetched streaming queries.
claimed_speedup: Survey arXiv 2506.06536v3, Table 6 (100M random string keys, single-threaded). PtrHash with lambda=3.0, linear, vec uses 2.990 bits/key, queries in 45 ns and builds in 141 ns/key. PtrHash with lambda=4.0, cubic, EF uses 2.118 bits/key, queries in 47 ns and builds in 358 ns/key. BBHash gamma=5.0 (6.870 bits/key) queries in 127 ns and builds in 157 ns/key. BBHash gamma=1.5 (3.293 bits/key) queries in 173 ns and builds in 273 ns/key. CMPH CHD lambda=4 (2.166 bits/key) queries in 356 ns and builds in 1,522 ns/key. PtrHash queries are about 2.7x-3.8x faster than BBHash and 7.6x-7.9x faster than CHD. Fast PtrHash builds 1.1x-1.9x faster than BBHash, and CHD builds 4.3x-10.8x slower than PtrHash (derived from page data). SEA 2025 paper arXiv 2502.15539v2, Table 2 (300M string keys, 6 threads): default PtrHash (2.40 bits/key) queries in 37 ns and 23 ns streaming. The fastest PTHash config (C-C) takes 77 ns, which gives the paper's stated 2.1x and 3.3x. CMPH CHD takes 542 ns, about 14.6x slower than default PtrHash (derived from page data). Paper Table 1 (1e9 integer keys): the MPHF for-loop query takes 12.5-14.2 ns only with the fast parameters (2.76-3.00 bits/key). It takes 20.0-21.7 ns with the default or compact parameters (2.09-2.62 bits/key). Streaming takes 8.6-9.7 ns in all configurations, and 8.6-8.8 ns with the Vec or CacheLineEF remap.
compiler_and_flags: Survey: GNU C++ 14.2.0 with -O3 -march=native (CMake Release), and Rust 1.85.0 in release mode with target-cpu=native. PtrHash is linked from the ptr_hash crate pinned at =1.1.0 through a Rust staticlib FFI contender. SEA paper: no compiler version is stated. The PtrHash repo builds with -C target-cpu=native (.cargo/config.toml on master) and a release profile with lto=thin.
hardware: Survey: Intel Core i7-11700 (8 cores, 16 threads), pinned to its 2.5 GHz base clock, Rocky Linux 9.5, Linux 5.14.0. SEA paper: Intel Core i7-10750H, 6 cores, hyper-threading disabled, frequency pinned to 2.6 GHz, 64 GiB DDR4-3200.
tradeoffs: Rust implementation; an unofficial, ambiguously-licensed C++ port exists (bassiounix/PtrHash-cc, made for an LLVM libc RFC) but has no independent benchmarks; CompactPtrHash trades ~2x slower construction for smaller size; needs sharding for keys that don't fit in RAM
caveats: PtrHash is a Rust crate with no C/C++ API. C++ use needs FFI, as MPHF-Experiments does. Neither source compares against std::unordered_map. The survey measured ptr_hash 1.1.0, and the current crate is 2.1.1. In survey Table 6, PHast and PHast+ (Rust) query slightly faster than PtrHash (38-44 ns vs 45-47 ns) at about 1.85-2.07 bits/key, so PtrHash is not the fastest-query MPHF there. Compact PtrHash builds slower than BBHash gamma=1.5 single-threaded (358 vs 273 ns/key). The paper's 2.1x and 3.3x are measured against the fastest PTHash configuration. Its 12 ns / 8 ns integer-key figures skip string hashing, and the 12 ns for-loop needs about 3 bits/key. The README large-input table was run at 3.6 GHz, not the paper's pinned 2.6 GHz. name: Sphinx
baseline: DHT (Delta Hash Table, a dynamic perfect hash table) / RSQF / Aleph Filter / Adaptive Aleph Filter (state-of-the-art fingerprint and perfect-hash indexes for log-structured hash tables / key-value stores)
workload: Average and tail-99 query/update/insertion latency and memory footprint (bits/entry) of an in-memory, Optane, and SSD-resident LSH-table index over up to 10^8 keys, against DHT, DHT-expandable, RSQF, Aleph Filter and Adaptive Aleph Filter C++ implementations
claimed_speedup: Abstract: about 2x lower query latency, update latency and memory footprint than the best alternatives. Fig. 6: zero false positives for queries to existing keys, and at most half the memory of the other baselines. In memory (Fig. 8), Sphinx has the lowest average and p99 query/update latency. Its average insertion is slightly slower than some baselines (read-before-write); Sphinx-4 (4 reserve bits) beats all baselines on every in-memory metric. On Optane, Sphinx variants are fastest. On SSD (Fig. 9), they match or beat all baselines, with only a slight gap to DHT-expandable under a uniform workload. Under skew at 90-99% cache hit rate, Sphinx is 10-35% faster than DHT-expandable (Fig. 10A).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.4.0 (benchmark/reproducibility.md, 'version installed or later'); -std=c++23 -O3 -march=native -mbmi2 (CMakeLists.txt). CMakeLists.txt also sets an RPATH to /usr/local/gcc-14.1.0 and has a commented-out GCC 14.1.0 compiler path.
hardware: Platform 1: Intel Xeon W7-2495X (24 cores/48 threads, 2.5GHz), 1.9MB L1/48MB L2/45MB L3, 512GB NVMe SSD (OS) + 2TB Samsung 980 Pro SSD (benchmark drive), Ubuntu 22.04; Platform 2: dual Intel Xeon Silver 4314 (32 cores/64 threads, 2.4GHz) with 256GB RAM + 496GB Intel Optane Persistent Memory 200 Series, Ubuntu 22.04
stars_or_usage: 22 stars; PVLDB vol. 18(11), pp. 4424-4437 (2025); the paper's PVLDB Artifact Availability section points to the repo
tradeoffs: Designed specifically as an in-memory index for LSH-table / log-structured key-value stores (not a general-purpose associative container); relies on x86 rank/select instructions (POPCNT, PEXT, TZCNT) for full speed; static succinct trie-based decoder is built for a fixed key set per block and expands via block-group splitting rather than arbitrary rehashing; DHT baseline was the authors' own C++ re-implementation since the original DHT code is closed-source
caveats: The baselines are LSH-table indexes and filters (DHT, RSQF, Aleph Filter), not std::unordered_map or MPHFs such as BBHash, CMPH or PTHash. DHT is the authors' own C++ reimplementation, because the original is closed-source. RSQF and Aleph Filter come from the Memento Filter codebase. Sphinx is a dynamic succinct perfect hash table (a key-to-payload index), not a static MPHF. It is x86-only and needs BMI2 PDEP/PEXT. The 2x headline comes from the abstract; the figures carry the per-experiment detail and there is no numeric table. The compiler version comes from the repo's reproducibility doc, not the paper, and the CMake RPATH points to GCC 14.1.0, so the exact compiler for the paper runs is not certain.

The README's 5-20 ns covers the bare MPHF only, not map or set lookups; benches/map_with_dict.rs records 75.814 ms per 1M MapWithDict<u64,u32> gets (~75.8 ns each, derived). Third-party PR #6: Set::contains and Map/MapWithDict get over 1M random u64 keys with u32 values, against Rust std HashMap/HashSet (FxHash and SipHash DefaultHasher) and rkyv 0.8 ArchivedHashMap.
claimed_speedup: README (first-party, no baseline row): Mphf query time 5-20 ns depending on parameters, number of keys and L1-L3 cache sizes; 2.10-2.71 bits/key. benches/mphf.rs doc comment (N=1M random u64, Mphf<32,8>): 14.372 ms per 1M gets at gamma 1.0 (2.10 bits/key) and 4.5959 ms at gamma 2.0 (2.72 bits/key), i.e. ~14.4 and ~4.6 ns/get (derived from page data). No first-party head-to-head against any baseline. Third-party unmerged PR #6 (result black_box fixed, N=1M u64, hardware unstated): Mphf get 26.267 ms (gamma 1.0) / 19.683 ms (gamma 2.0) per 1M; Set contains 26.454 ms vs std HashSet+FxHash 14.704 ms (~1.8x slower) and vs std HashSet+DefaultHasher (SipHash) 34.877 ms (~1.32x faster; ~1.06x at equal hasher, 32.839 ms); u64->u32 get: new Map 37.293 ms and MapWithDict 45.406 ms vs std HashMap+FxHash 18.518 / 18.921 ms (~2.0x / ~2.4x slower); archived Map get 41.039 ms vs rkyv ArchivedHashMap 37.373 ms (~1.1x slower). tradeoffs: Immutable map/set only (no post-construction inserts); Rust crate, so C++ use requires an FFI boundary; requires a value dictionary (MapWithDict) for arbitrary values rather than native insert semantics; construction-time vs. query-time tradeoff tunable via a gamma parameter

The README's 5-20 ns is for the bare Mphf::get, not for MapWithDict or Set lookups (~75.8 ns per MapWithDict get in the repo's own bench comment, derived). The original benches black_box only the key and do not black_box the result. Unmerged third-party PR #6 fixes this and measures 19.7-26.3 ns per Mphf get instead of 4.6-14.4 ns (hardware unstated, fat-LTO profile disabled, so not a like-for-like rerun). benches/set.rs has a std HashSet harness but publishes no results, and it still uses the fxhash crate that was removed from Cargo.toml in 2024-10 (issue #5), so it likely does not build as-is. The real advantage is memory (2.10-2.72 bits/key for the MPHF). No C++ baseline was tested. name: constmap
workload: Every key of a 1,000,000-key string-to-uint64 dataset (keys 'key-%d') is looked up exactly once in random order, from a query buffer allocated in query order (makeQueryOrder in constmap_test.go). The Scaling table runs one pass at 10K, 100K, 1M and 10M keys. The README's batched MapMany numbers compare only against a loop over ConstMap.Map, not against Go's map.
claimed_speedup: README 'Performance gains' table (Apple M4 Max, 1,000,000 keys, every key queried once in random order): ConstMap 8.7 ns/op vs Go map[string]uint64 46 ns/op. The README states this as 5.3x over the whole key set, and 1.2x over only 256 queries. VerifiedConstMap, the variant that detects missing keys like a Go map does, takes 15 ns/op, about 3.1x (derived from page data). Memory is 9.0 bytes/key for ConstMap and 18 for VerifiedConstMap vs 48 for the Go map, about 5.3x and 2.7x less (derived from page data). The README 'Scaling' table (TestLookupAndMemoryTable, one pass, M4 Max) reports ConstMap / VerifiedConstMap / Go map at 10K keys as 9.4 / 10.4 / 14.8 ns (about 1.6x / 1.4x), at 1M keys as 12.5 / 18.6 / 51.1 ns (about 4.1x / 2.7x), and at 10M keys as 34.8 / 41.3 / 70.1 ns (about 2.0x / 1.7x). All of these ratios are derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: Go gc toolchain via go test. The Go version is not stated: go.mod declares only a go 1.22 minimum, and CI uses 'stable'. The README gives `go test -bench=. -benchmem` and recommends `-count=5 -benchtime=3s`, but does not say which flags produced the headline table. The batch table uses medians of `-benchtime 3s -count 3`. The Go-map benchmark code is constmap_test.go (BenchmarkConstMap, BenchmarkVerifiedConstMap, BenchmarkGoMap, TestLookupAndMemoryTable with RUN_HEAVY_MEMORY_TESTS=1). batch_bench_test.go, hashbatch_bench_test.go and paired_test.go hold the batching and paired-layout benchmarks, which have no Go-map baseline.
hardware: Apple M4 Max for every Go-map comparison. The Intel Xeon Gold 6548N appears only in the MapMany-vs-loop batching, paired-vs-split layout and serialization numbers, none of which include Go's map.
tradeoffs: Immutable: keys must be known at construction time (build-then-query), so it targets static/compile-time-known key sets like std::unordered_map replacements built from a fixed keyword set, not general dynamic maps. Baseline is Go's built-in map[string]uint64, not C++ std::unordered_map, so this is evidence for the binary-fuse-filter static-map technique, not a direct C++ stdlib win. ConstMap stores no keys and returns an undefined value for absent keys. VerifiedConstMap (15 ns vs 46 ns, about 3.1x) is the semantically comparable variant. The margin depends on cache residency: 1.2x over 256 queries vs 5.3x over the full 1M key set, and about 1.6x at 10K and 2.0x at 10M keys in the Scaling table. Construction is slower than building a Go map, which the README states but does not quantify. The headline table (8.7 vs 46 ns) and the Scaling table (12.5 vs 51.1 ns) differ at the same 1M size. The 2026-03-29 launch blog post reported 7.4 vs 20 ns (about 2.7x) under an earlier methodology; the README switched to random-order lookups on 2026-08-27 (commit d2e538f5).

Batched, 2000 batches of 2000 keys, cold cache: a dict list comprehension takes 148.7 ns/op. name: fastcpp::phf (developer source)
workload: 200k keyword lookups against a 92-key C++20 keyword table (fastcpp::phf, a compiler-built perfect hash baked into .rodata) compared to std::unordered_map<string_view,uint16_t>, measured separately for all-hit, all-miss, and 1:8-mixed-hit-rate corpora.
claimed_speedup: 6.98x on all-hit lookups (3.327ns vs 23.208ns/op), 6.70x on all-miss (3.02ns vs 20.243ns), 5.76x on mixed 1:8 (4.903ns vs 28.235ns) -- verbatim from results/fastest.json. Also beats phmap::flat_hash_map (Apache-2.0, vendored in-repo) 3.7x and frozen::unordered_map 3.5-3.7x on the same static workload, though the frozen comparison is weaker evidence (see caveats).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 13.3.0, -O2 -g -DNDEBUG -std=c++20 -march=native (CMake RelWithDebInfo, 'release' preset)
hardware: Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz (AVX2, SSE4.2, BMI2), 4 cores, Ubuntu 24.04 / Linux 6.18 -- a shared cloud VM; the repo's own results file warns absolute ns move between runs on this host (ratios within a run are what is claimed as stable)
tradeoffs: Only usable when the key set is closed at compile time (keywords, opcodes, enum labels) -- no runtime insert/delete. The shipped default comparison policy (std::memcmp) is not the fastest one measured: compare_policy::overread16 is 1.44x faster still but requires 16 readable bytes at the query pointer, so it is opt-in rather than default. Table size scales with key count and is baked into .rodata, growing binary size. Requires a C++20-capable compiler (gcc 13+/clang 17+/MSVC 19.35+) for the constexpr search; clang needs a much larger constexpr-step budget than gcc for the same search.
caveats: The repo is PRIVATE and readable only with an authenticated gh CLI, so the benchmark code is not public and the entry cannot be Tier A. List readers will get a 404 on repo_url and benchmark_url. It has 0 stars. It is a single-author project: all 13 commits are authored by 'Claude' with Claude co-author trailers, and nobody outside has reviewed it. The CPU is given only as 'Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz' (shared cloud VM, no SKU). The results file warns that absolute ns vary between runs (3.42 vs 5.24 ns for the same lookup) and that only ratios within one run are meaningful. name: triehash
workload: Each of the 82 field names from Debian Packages/Sources files is hashed 1,000,000 times back-to-back. hashbench also probes 3 extra words: Hallo, PaCKage, PackageXXX. Throughput is the summed word bytes divided by the total ns, reported in GB/s. The table has 7 host/arch columns on 5 hosts: jak-x230 and backup (amd64), asachi.d.o (arm64/armel/armhf), plummer.d.o (ppc64el), and eller.d.o (mipsel). Other competitors are re2c, djb hash variants, and APT's AlphaHash.
claimed_speedup: README Performance table (GB/s, higher is better). On jak-x230 (amd64, Core i5-3320M), Trie is 2.4 vs gperf 1.3 case-sensitive [~1.85x, derived from page data], and Trie (*) is 2.2 vs gperf (*) 0.7 case-insensitive [~3.1x, derived from page data]. Comparing like with like across all 7 host/arch columns, Trie is ~1.85x (x230) to ~5x (plummer ppc64el, 2.0 vs 0.4) faster than gperf case-sensitive. Trie (*) is ~2x (eller mipsel, 0.2 vs 0.1, coarsely rounded) to ~4x (asachi arm64, 0.8 vs 0.2) faster than gperf (*) case-insensitive [derived from page data].
compiler_and_flags: Per the julian-klode/hashbench Makefile: gcc (CC := $(CROSS)-gcc; version not stated). CFLAGS ?= -O2 -g -fPIE -fstack-protector-strong -Wformat -Werror=format-security, and LDFLAGS ?= --static. The gperf baseline is generated with `gperf --includes --pic --readonly-tables`, plus --ignore-case for gperf (*). The README notes also point to gcc bug 77729 (extra zero-extend instructions).
hardware: jak-x230: Intel Core i5-3320M (stated in the README legend). backup (amd64) and the Debian porterboxes asachi.debian.org (arm64/armel/armhf), plummer.debian.org (ppc64el) and eller.debian.org (mipsel) are named by hostname only, with no CPU model. The legend's 'barriere has an Opteron 23xx' refers to an earlier table; barriere is not in the current table.
stars_or_usage: 49 stars; used in APT (Debian package manager)
tradeoffs: Order-preserving (unlike most minimal perfect hash schemes), which trades some construction flexibility for keeping key order in the output table. Generator only handles a fixed key set known at generation time (codegen tool, like gperf, not a runtime container).
caveats: The benchmark code is not in the triehash repo. It lives in github.com/julian-klode/hashbench (MIT, 0 stars, last commit 2016-10-06), which the author's 2016-09-25 blog post links. Its Makefile and render-results.py produce exactly the README table layout, and the table landed in triehash the same day (2016-10-06). The gcc version is not stated. Only jak-x230 (Core i5-3320M) has a CPU model; the other hosts are named by hostname only. The method favors branchy switch-based code: each word is hashed 1,000,000 times in a row, so the branch predictor is fully trained and the cache is hot. The gperf baseline was generated with --pic --readonly-tables rather than gperf defaults. The mipsel figures (0.1-0.2 GB/s) are too coarsely rounded for meaningful ratios. The numbers date from 2016. re2c matchers and APT's unrolled AlphaHash (apt (**), 2.3 GB/s on x230) also come close to Trie. triehash is a Perl script (GitHub language: Shell) that generates C code, and the generated C is directly callable from C++. The last commit on main is 2019-04-16; the debian/master packaging branch has commits up to 2022-12-14. Both are more than 3 years old, so the project is abandoned. APT uses triehash: apt-pkg/CMakeLists.txt runs it with --ignore-case to generate tagfile-keys (verified on the Debian/apt GitHub mirror).
